item.title: Analyst and AI: Three Tools That Turn Chaos into Requirements
item.description:
We're working on a large project with dozens of integrations, hundreds of business scenarios, Confluence documentation, and now AI-generated descriptions of business scenarios directly in repositories. This is great for getting acquainted with the project, but it doesn't cover the whole picture when working on a specific enhancement. Therefore, our analyst team has started creating our own AI agents: we gather relevant Git repositories, customer requirements documents (BFD), and meeting notes into a folder, and then design and analyze with the agent. In this article, we'll break down the full pipeline: how we prepare data for the AI agent, provide it with context, and then transform the analysis results into a ready-to-use Technical Specification (ChTZ). Without proper input preparation, even the smartest agent will produce nonsense, and the Markdown output still needs to be formatted into a corporate .docx. Read on

item.title: Video Neural Network Ranking: Compared 12 Models on a Single Prompt (October 2026)
item.description:
Twelve video neural networks were run on a single prompt: 8 seconds, 720p, one generation per model. Luma Ray 3.14 came out on top with a total score of 9.1 out of 10, two minutes, 5 tokens, and was the cheapest. Seedance 2.5 produced the best image quality but was the most expensive: 138.7 tokens, 27 times more than the leader. Read more

item.title: One and a Half Months of Accelerating MoE on a GTX 1660 SUPER: The Native llama.cpp Flag Won
item.description:
I'm a thermomechanic, head of a department in a design organization, not a programmer. Since August, I've been tinkering with a llama.cpp fork: I want large MoE models to run properly on a regular home PC with a 6GB graphics card, 24GB of RAM, and a SATA drive. The testbed was gpt-oss-20b. The result so far is disappointing: the native -fit flag won, being 2.44 times faster than the usual -ngl 99 on a long prompt, and my own optimizations on top of it yielded nothing. However, along the way, I've collected a good set of ways speed measurements can be misleading, and a couple of settings that will be useful for any owner of a small graphics card. Read on

item.title: How to Feed a Large Project to a Neural Network Without Overfeeding: What I Learned While Agents Read My Code
item.description:
A year ago, I was copying files into a chat with a neural network one by one. Now, agents read the project themselves via an MCP server, and a month of observing them has been more surprising than all previous work: why a text tree is more expensive for a model than JSON, why the build folder cannot be skipped by name, how to hide a password without breaking the surrounding code, and what an agent actually does with context when no one is controlling it. item.title: LLM Development in 2026: Skills, Cases, Requirements
item.description:
Hello, Habr! I am a senior software engineer at Finam and the author of the "LLM Developer" course at Hexlet. We'll talk about LLM development practices and everyday details: who needs RAG, whether it's necessary to work with large models, what the LLM development market is like, and how to enter the profession – what skills are needed, how to search, and how much to ask for. If you're too lazy to read, I've covered all of this in a video. This material is for those who prefer letters to movies. Around 2024, the world began to understand the direction of AI and its applications. In 2025-2026, Russia also woke up: "Goodness, artificial intelligence can be used!" It's not really intelligence, but who cares: everyone wants to use it at work. How? We don't know. For what purpose? We don't know. Business doesn't quite understand what it needs – but it needs it because "it's a revolution, Johnny!" In reality, it is a revolution, but like any revolution, you need to understand how, for what, and where to use it. Your CEO might say: "We want to use artificial intelligence everywhere: integrating it into development, CI/CD, assessment, code review, task assignment, and assistant work." AI can indeed be applied in all these areas, even allowing the CEO to order coffee via a chatbot. Read more

item.title: The Debate Over Open Model Cyber-Risks is Broken
item.description:
Nathan Lambert (Interconnects) on why the debate over banning open-weight models leads to a lose-lose situation. Most documented attacks so far have been via closed models, Anthropic's report on GLM-5.3 sidesteps the main issue, and Chinese labs assess risks differently. The author's conclusion: those who want to ban open weights for safety must also be prepared to ban public APIs of frontier models. Read more →

Original Russian article on Habr

item.title: AI Reaches PLCs: What Engineering Assistants Can Do
item.description:
AI in Python, C++, JavaScript, and other languages is already commonplace. Habr discusses this extensively, often debating how a programmer's job should look now. But what about PLC programming? At first glance, it's a similar task. There are languages, variables, conditions, timers, and function blocks. Why not ask a model to write a pump or conveyor control algorithm? You can ask, but it's not that simple yet. More and more specialized tools are emerging that read PLC projects, explain LAD, generate ST code, and in some cases, even start compilation themselves. However, working with them still has its nuances. In this article, I've tried to understand what AI tools for PLC code are today, what they actually do, and where all this is heading. Read on

item.title: One office instead of five services: why I'm creating 121ai for those who work 1-on-1
item.description:
In previous articles, I wrote about my journey in IT, and now I want to tell you about my project. For those who don't know me yet, let's get acquainted. My name is Denis, I've been in IT for 22 years: I've gone from developer to development team lead. For many years, I've been building teams, mentoring people, and implementing automation, including AI-based solutions. Therefore, when my wife, an ICF coach and system analyst with 18 years of IT experience, showed me how much time "helping" professionals spend on everything surrounding the session itself, I immediately recognized a familiar pattern – what I encounter daily in my work and try to automate: too many tools where one is needed. That's how we started building 121ai together. Read more

item.title: Why I Returned to a 200K Context Window with Claude
item.description:
In the spring, a $100 subscription was enough for all my pet project tasks. The idea of fully exhausting the five-hour token limit seemed like a challenge. By early summer, I was managing it well, but by August, limits were only sufficient for technical design, delaying implementation until the next week. I'd start tasks and use up the weekly limit in about 3 days. In September, I had a $200 subscription, but even its limits weren't insurmountable. Friends and colleagues mentioned they were already on maximum Claude and GPT subscriptions and planning to get a third! Pouring more money seemed like a dead end, so I started looking into optimizing token consumption. The main reason wasn't the complexity of tasks or code volume, but simple daily convenience. Read more
